title: Clean Code
author: Marcy Knook
markdown:
Reading Robert C. Martin's *Clean Code* and learning more about code smells gave me a boost in my understanding of reading and writing code. It gave me a stronger basis for explaining why I write code the way I do. I enjoyed reading it and feel that it will help me in code reviews and make me a better programmer in general. Seeing the different smells written down and making my own summary really helped me understand them and appreciate the value of doing things well.

I was not fully aware that having too many function arguments, or using output arguments, could be code smells. Although I did not use output arguments myself, I have used my fair share of flag arguments.

My colleague's arguments for removing author names and dates from files also make more sense now. For some reason, this information appeared in scripts within our codebase. Another habit of mine was adding comments explaining what a function did, just because. I think I have moved away from that because I believe most of the code I write explains itself nowadays, as it should.

Besides that, I am definitely starting to see the usefulness of developing as though the functionality I need already exists. A bad habit of mine, though, is trying to write everything out starting with the variables, rather than starting with the functionality I want to have. That is definitely something I will be focusing on in the future.

I don't know whose quote it was, but it reminded me of: "Everything that's worth doing is worth doing properly."

I think my next post will be about test-driven development or using SonarQube.

title: Learning to develop with Codex
author: Marcy Knook
markdown:
These past few weeks, I've learnt to make more use of an LLM in my development process. I've connected Codex within my development environment and have been learning how to give it enough context and explain clearly what I want it to do. I've mainly been using it within my personal portfolio, where I can experiment without much risk if something goes wrong. So far, it has been useful and has not caused many problems, although I've noticed that the available usage goes faster than one might expect when using it for larger development tasks.

I'm learning this because it almost feels wrong not to. These tools are becoming more capable and more integrated into development workflows, and I think completely ignoring them could eventually mean falling behind. At the same time, I do not want to use Codex as something that simply writes code for me. I still need to understand and review what it produces.

Using Codex is also showing me that I still have a long way to go in consistently applying testing, code quality standards and a structured development process. If requirements or conventions are unclear, Codex can make assumptions that I need to catch during review, preferably before they make it into production.

I therefore see Codex mostly as another development tool. If I get better at giving it context, setting constraints and reviewing its output, I think it can improve both the speed and effectiveness with which we develop what customers need.
